current_episode.title: Who Moves Up, and Who's Pushed Out, in Pete Hegseth's Military

guest.bio_context: Greg Jaffe is a journalist at The New York Times who has been covering the military since 1999, on and off, spanning 26 years. He co-reported this story with colleague Kate Kelly, investigating the hiring and firing patterns within Pete Hegseth's Pentagon. He describes this period as unprecedented in the 26 years he has covered the military, stating he cannot think of anything remotely close to the scale of the current purge.

context.real_quote: When you start firing people for political reasons, it's not just the person you fire, but it's the message that sends throughout the entire force that if you want to move up, there are political litmus tests that you have to pass through.

pending_qa.q: What was the Inspector General complaint against Admiral Daryl Caudill and how was it resolved?
pending_qa.r: The Inspector General complaint against Caudill, approximately a year old when his nomination was being considered, centered on remarks he made to sailors at an awards banquet during a discussion of the Navy's sexual assault awareness program. He used analogies suggesting victims bear partial responsibility for assaults, prompting complaints from sailors who heard the remarks. The IG ultimately concluded he had done nothing wrong, clearing the path for his nomination to proceed to the White House.

pending_qa.q: What role did lawyer Tim Parlatore play in the Caudill nomination process?
pending_qa.r: When Caudill needed to address the Inspector General complaint, he retained lawyer Tim Parlatore, who had previously represented other naval officers in IG complaints and had also represented Secretary Hegseth when Hegseth was accused of sexual assault. At the time of Caudill's nomination process, Parlatore was working as a special advisor inside the Pentagon, further deepening the network of connections between Caudill and Hegseth.

pending_qa.q: Why is the politicization of military promotions considered dangerous for national security?
pending_qa.r: Greg Jaffe argues that when people are fired for political reasons, it sends a message throughout the entire force that advancement requires passing political litmus tests, which can cause officers to make important military decisions based on what will please their superiors rather than on sound military judgment. He emphasizes that effective warfare requires officers who can provide unvarnished military advice even when it is unpopular, and that you want the best warfighters promoted rather than the most politically aligned ones.

pending_qa.q: What is the current status of women in senior Navy leadership under Pete Hegseth?
pending_qa.r: For the first time in at least a decade, if not longer, there will be no women nominated to admiral rank under Hegseth. Women currently make up approximately 21 percent of the Navy, meaning the leadership increasingly looks less like the force it oversees. Jaffe notes this is both a loss of role models for young female officers coming up through the ranks and heartbreaking for senior female officers like Franchetti who fought hard to reach their positions.

pending_qa.q: What was the combat exclusion ban and how did it affect Lisa Franchetti's early Navy career?
pending_qa.r: The combat exclusion ban was a policy in place when Franchetti joined the Navy in the 1980s that prevented women from serving on combat ships or in combat aircraft, severely limiting their ability to rise to high ranks. In 1989, Franchetti was one of only 184 female surface warfare officers in the entire United States Navy. The ban was lifted by President Clinton in the 1990s, which opened up opportunities for Franchetti to command combat vessels and ultimately reach the top of the Navy.

pending_qa.q: How did President Biden's selection of Franchetti differ from Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin's recommendation?
pending_qa.r: Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin's first choice for Chief of Naval Operations was Sam Paparo, a senior Navy officer with extensive experience in the Pacific. Biden overruled Austin and selected Franchetti instead, keeping Paparo focused on U.S. Indo-Pacific Command given his experience with China-related challenges. Jaffe notes this was unusual but not unheard of, as the president ultimately holds the authority to make this appointment, and Biden was interested both in her qualifications and in making history by appointing the first female Chief of Naval Operations.
